title: The First Thanksgiving: What the 1621 Letter Actually Says
subtitle: A harvest feast in a few lines of a letter, and how the name, the date, and the picture came later

segments.text: Pilgrims in tall black hats. Native guests at a long table. A roast turkey, and pumpkin pie. This is the First Thanksgiving, as millions of Americans picture it every November. But the only surviving written eyewitness account of that feast, in 1621, is a few lines in a letter. Those lines never call the feast a thanksgiving. And they never mention a turkey.

In this episode, we read that letter, follow how a harvest feast became "the First Thanksgiving," and look at a painting, made nearly three centuries later, that helped give us the picture we know today.

In December 1621, Edward Winslow, one of the English settlers at Plymouth, wrote a letter to a friend in England. It was printed in London the next year, in a small book now known as Mourt's Relation.

After the harvest, he wrote, the governor sent four men out fowling, so that they might rejoice together after gathering the fruits of their labors. Many of the Native people came, among them their greatest king, Massasoit, with some ninety men. For three days, the settlers entertained and feasted them, and the guests went out and killed five deer.

This short account tells us only so much. Fowl, which may have included ducks, geese, or turkeys. Venison, brought by Massasoit's men. Three days. Massasoit and about ninety men, and about fifty English settlers, the survivors of their first winter.

The colony's governor, William Bradford, later wrote that there was a great store of wild turkeys that autumn. But that passage describes the season's hunting, not the feast itself. And his history stayed in manuscript until 1856.

For the settlers, a day of thanksgiving was something else: a solemn religious day, set apart to thank God for a particular blessing. In 1623, during a long drought, Plymouth first held a day of fasting and prayer. Rain came. Later, they set apart another day, a day of thanksgiving. Winslow's letter of 1621 does not use that word for the harvest feast.
The feast also brought together allies. That spring, Massasoit and the settlers had promised peace, and to help each other if attacked. That autumn, the same people shared one feast.

In 1841, the historian Alexander Young reprinted Winslow's letter in a book of Pilgrim documents, and added a short note: this was the first Thanksgiving, the harvest festival of New England. He added that they "no doubt" feasted on wild turkey. The letter itself does not say so.

Meanwhile, the magazine editor Sarah Josepha Hale was asking for one national day of Thanksgiving. In a letter to President Abraham Lincoln in 1863, she wrote that she had urged the idea for fifteen years. That October, in the middle of the Civil War, Lincoln called on Americans to keep the last Thursday of November as a day of thanksgiving and praise. His proclamation does not mention the Pilgrims.

Later still, painters filled in the picture. In the early twentieth century, one popular painting showed long tables, white collars, and Native guests in feathered headdresses of the Great Plains, far from New England. It was painted nearly three centuries after the feast.
Today, the day holds more than one meaning. At Cole's Hill in Plymouth, the United American Indians of New England has held a National Day of Mourning on Thanksgiving Day since 1970.

So what happened in 1621? A three-day harvest feast, shared by English settlers and Massasoit's people, with fowl and venison. The letter that records it does not call it a thanksgiving. The name, the November date, and the familiar picture were added later.
Every story has an origin. Sometimes, it begins with a few lines in a letter.
